title: Lateral Ankle Sprain
case: Case: A 22-year-old basketball player rolled his right ankle 5 days ago. He walked off the court with a limp. Ottawa rules are negative (no bone tenderness, could take four steps). There is swelling and bruising over the outer ankle, tenderness over the ATFL, a positive anterior drawer with a soft end-feel, and a negative squeeze test. Neurovascular status is normal.

Working diagnosis: grade 2 lateral ankle sprain. Plan: brace support, early walking, range and strength work, balance training, graded return to hopping and cutting, tape or brace for return to sport, reassess weekly.
qa: Why test the ligaments 4 to 5 days later instead of immediately? Swelling, pain and guarding hide laxity in the first hours, so the delayed examination is more informative [Ref - to verify].
Why use the Ottawa rules first? They help decide who needs an X-ray, so fractures are not missed and unnecessary imaging is avoided.
Pain above the ankle and a positive squeeze test. What does that suggest? A syndesmosis injury, which often needs a longer recovery and medical review.
Why not rest the ankle for several weeks? Prolonged immobilisation can delay recovery. Early protected loading and exercise are generally better [Ref - to verify].
Why train balance after the swelling goes down? Proprioception and control are often reduced after a sprain and training lowers the risk of repeat injury [Ref - to verify].

tests.name: Ottawa ankle rules (screen for fracture before testing ligaments)

fields.Purpose: Decide whether an X-ray is needed after an acute ankle or midfoot injury
fields.Ankle X-ray series is suggested if there: Bone tenderness at the back edge or tip of either malleolus (along the lower 6 cm), or inability to bear weight for four steps both immediately after injury and at examination
fields.Foot X-ray series is suggested if there: Bone tenderness at the base of the 5th metatarsal or at the navicular, or inability to bear weight for four steps
fields.Positive: Any listed finding; refer for imaging
fields.Negative: None of the findings; fracture is unlikely
fields.Limits: Designed for adults and older children; high sensitivity but not perfect, with a low false-negative rate when used correctly [Ref - to verify]

tests.name: Anterior drawer test of the ankle

fields.Position: Sitting with the knee bent and the foot relaxed, or supine; ankle in about 10 to 20 degrees of plantar flexion
fields.Therapist position: One hand holds the lower shin (tibia) still from the front; the other cups the heel from behind
fields.Action: Pull the heel forward while pushing the tibia backward. Compare the amount of movement and the end-feel with the other ankle
fields.Positive: Increased forward movement of the foot, a soft end-feel, or a dimple (suction sign) over the front of the outer ankle
fields.Negative: Similar to the other side, firm end-feel
fields.Limits: More accurate when performed 4 to 5 days after the injury than immediately, because pain and swelling cause guarding [Ref - to verify]; comparison with the other side is essential
fields.Errors: Pulling with the toes or foot held tense; not stabilising the tibia; testing a very painful ankle

fields.Purpose: Test the CFL (in neutral) and ATFL (in plantar flexion)
fields.Position: Lying or sitting; ankle in neutral for the CFL
fields.Action: Hold the lower shin still and tilt the heel inward (inversion stress); compare with the other side
fields.Positive: More opening than the other side or a soft end-feel
fields.Limits: Reliability varies; often painful in the acute phase

fields.Position and action: Squeeze the shin and calf bones together at mid-calf
fields.Positive: Pain in the area above the ankle

fields.Position and action: Sitting, knee bent to 90 degrees; stabilise the shin and rotate the foot outward
Press along the front of the syndesmosis

redFlags.Finding: Ottawa rule positive, deformity, or severe pain
Pale, cold or pulseless foot, or severe swelling with intense pain
Positive calf squeeze test or palpable gap in the Achilles
redFlags.Immediate action: Refer same day or next day

redFlags.Finding: Pain above the ankle with positive squeeze test
Hot red swollen ankle with fever
Pain not improving after about 6 weeks, or recurrent swelling and catching

manual.name: Mobilization with movement (talocrural glide for dorsiflexion)
manual.why: May improve dorsiflexion range and short-term function [Ref - to verify]
manual.application: Weight-bearing lunge, apply a gentle posterior glide of the talus with a belt or hands, repeated pain-free

manualNotes: Preferred starting choice: early protected loading and exercise. Manual therapy is optional for short-term range and comfort. Avoid forcing inversion stress through an injured ligament.

exercise.Exercises: Ankle alphabet, pumps, gentle dorsiflexion and plantar flexion, walking with support
exercise.Progress when: Walking without a limp, swelling reducing

exercise.Exercises: Band eversion and inversion, calf raises, toe raises, sit-to-stand
exercise.Progress when: Pain-free, strength near the other side

exercise.Exercises: Single-leg stand (eyes open, then eyes closed, then on a cushion), wobble board, reach drills
Hopping, landing, cutting, figure-8 running, sport drills

exerciseNotes: Principle: early functional treatment (protection with a brace or tape, early walking, and progressive exercise) gives better results than prolonged immobilisation for most sprains [Ref - to verify]. A short period of support (for example a few days up to a few weeks in more severe sprains) can be used for comfort.

Return to sport criteria (example): full pain-free range, near-normal strength, balance equal to the other side, no swelling, confidence in hopping and cutting, and passing sport-specific tests. Many athletes use tape or a brace for a period after return, which reduces recurrence in people with a history of sprains [Ref - to verify]. No fixed date is set.
Recurrence prevention: continuing balance and strengthening exercise lowers the risk of repeated sprains [Ref - to verify].

modalities.name: Brace or taping
modalities.indicated: Recommended for support and return to sport
modalities.comment: Choose based on comfort and access [Ref - to verify]

modalityNotes: The older RICE rule (rest, ice, compression, elevation) is now often replaced by approaches that include protection and early optimal loading [Ref - to verify]. Avoid prolonged rest or immobilisation.
pathway: Any emergency or urgent flag? Yes: act as in Section G.
Ottawa rules positive? Yes: refer for imaging.
Ottawa negative, lateral pain and swelling, and positive anterior drawer or talar tilt, particularly 4 to 5 days after injury? Yes: working diagnosis is lateral ankle sprain.
Positive syndesmosis tests? Yes: treat as a possible syndesmosis injury and seek medical review.
Otherwise: begin protected loading and exercise.
Acute (first days): screen flags and the Ottawa rules, protect, reduce swelling, begin early gentle movement and weight-bearing.
Early rehabilitation: restore range, begin strengthening and balance.
Middle: progress to hopping, landing and change of direction.
